title: Carabid trends at 12 UK ECN sites in 1994-2008 did not predict trends in 2009-2015, and species thermal affinity did not explain the declines
abstract: We used UK Environmental Change Network (ECN) pitfall data for ground beetles (Carabidae) at 12 sites in 1992-2015. We did an out-of-sample test of the 1994-2008 declines that Brooks et al. (2012) reported. We also tested one climate explanation: cool-climate species must decrease more than warm-climate species. Annual indices controlled for valid trap-days, transects, season coverage and the activity response of the catch to the temperature of each two-week trap period. In 1994-2008 the median trend of 211 species-site series was -4.4% per year (95% CI -7.2 to -2.3). In 2009-2015 it was +1.7% per year (95% CI -3.8 to +9.3; 118 series, 10 sites). The slopes of the same series in the two periods had no correlation (Spearman -0.09). For 157 series, the extrapolated 1994-2008 trend forecast the 2009-2015 catch worse than the 2004-2008 level (skill -0.64, CI -1.02 to -0.36). A placebo test inside 1994-2008 gave the same failure (skill -1.08). The median 2009-2015 catch stayed 17% below the 2004-2008 level. For all carabids, the catch at the 7 sites with clear declines was equal to or above the extrapolated decline. A species temperature index from GBIF occupancy and 1961-1990 GHCN-CAMS temperature did not predict trends in either period or in cool or warm site groups (+0.010 and +0.017 per C, all p > 0.09). The community temperature index had no trend. A 1 C warmer trap period caught 9.1% more beetles, but this bias did not change the conclusions. Limitations: the out-of-sample period is short (4-7 years), pitfall catches measure activity-density, and other causes such as management were not tested.
